name: turbovec (Rust TurboQuant vector index with Python bindings)
baseline: FAISS IndexPQFastScan (C++) at a matched bit rate (m = d sub-quantizers, 4-bit codes in the published 4-bit script); FAISS IndexPQ (LUT256, nbits=8) for the recall comparison
workload: Nearest-neighbour search over 100K quantized embeddings (OpenAI text-embedding-3 d=1536 and d=3072, GloVe d=200), k=64, 1K queries, median of 5 runs, 2-bit and 4-bit, single- and multi-threaded, on ARM and x86 cloud VMs.
claimed_speedup: README: 'searches them 4.4x faster than FAISS, at matching recall'; '4.4x FAISS FastScan at 4-bit and 2.2x at 2-bit, on ARM and x86'; README table: search 4-bit '3.8-5.1x faster across the eight cells (ARM 4.0x, x86 4.9x)', search 2-bit '1.8-2.5x faster (ARM 2.05x, x86 2.35x)'. Project-recorded losses: whole-file save 1.0-1.4x slower and load to first search 1.0-1.5x slower than FAISS.
compiler_and_flags: Rust release build (cargo run --release); x86_64 builds target x86-64-v2 via .cargo/config.toml with #[target_feature]-gated AVX-512 and AVX2 kernels chosen at runtime (README). FAISS version, build and flags are not stated (benchmarks/suite scripts import the Python faiss module).
hardware: GCP c4a-standard-8 (Google Axion, ARM, 8 vCPUs) and GCP c3-standard-8 (Intel Xeon Platinum 8481C, Sapphire Rapids, 8 vCPUs), from docs/benchmarks.md.
tradeoffs: Brute-force scan of every vector with no graph index, so query cost grows linearly with corpus size (README advises another index for hundreds of millions of vectors); lossy 2- and 4-bit quantization; Python-facing API; atomic save and load are slower than FAISS write_index/read_index.
caveats: Not the same algorithm: turbovec runs a staged search (one bit plane scanned with a table kernel, shortlist ranked on lower planes, best candidates rescored exactly) while the speed comparator is FAISS IndexPQFastScan with no refinement, so 'matching recall' rests on separate recall tables against FAISS IndexPQ (docs/benchmarks.md: the calibrated index trails FAISS by 0.7 points at R@1 for d=1536 4-bit, and GloVe d=200 is the harder regime). Author-run on cloud VMs; FAISS version, build and thread settings are not stated; timings include Python call overhead. The x86 kernel adapts FAISS FastScan's pack layout. Vector search sits at the edge of the numerics-and-arrays category; the orchestrator may re-file it.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/simd?l=rust topic page (turbovec listed first), then README and docs/benchmarks.md and benchmarks/suite/speed_d1536_4bit_x86_mt.py
why_faster: Staged bit-plane search: a sign plane is scanned with a nibble-LUT table kernel adapted from FAISS FastScan, a shortlist is ranked on the lower planes, then rescored exactly; AVX-512/AVX2/NEON kernels are selected at runtime.

name: ipnsort and driftsort (Rust std sort_unstable and sort) in Voultapher/sort-research-rs
baseline: C++ std::sort in libstdc++ (gcc 13.2.1), libc++ (clang 16.0.6) and MSVC STL; also Intel x86-simd-sort (AVX-512, C++), Google vqsort and cpp_pdqsort in the AVX-512 analysis
workload: In-place sorting of u64 arrays (10k elements in the std comparison; sizes up to 10m in the AVX-512 analysis) over patterns ascending, descending, random, random_d20, random_p5, random_s95, random_z1 and saws, in hot and cold (L1i and branch-predictor flushed) runs.
claimed_speedup: sort_safety writeup (graphs only, no ratio in the text): 'the current Rust standard library unstable sort implementation outperforms the C++ standard library counterparts'. Text numbers from the AVX-512 analysis against C++ x86-simd-sort (intel_avx512): ipnsort is '~15x times faster on Windows and ~19x on Linux' on random_p5 at input size 10m; on already-sorted input ipnsort is '~20x faster on Windows and ~15x on Linux' at 100k and '~10x faster on Windows and ~16x on Linux' at 10m. The same page says a headline 'Rust std sort is 15x faster than C++ std sort' is 'not an honest representation'.
compiler_and_flags: std comparison (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Voultapher/sort-research-rs/HEAD/writeup/sort_safety/text.md): rustc 1.75.0-nightly (2023-10-03) --release with lto=thin, clang 16.0.6, gcc 13.2.1, native build settings in build.rs at commit 190b3ec (build.rs not opened). AVX-512 analysis: rustc 1.69.0-nightly, clang 15.0.1 / 14.0.6, MSVC 19.31; manually vectorized sorts built with clang -march=native.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X (Zen 3, boost enabled) for the std comparison; Intel Core i9-10980XE (Windows) and Intel Xeon Gold 6154 (Linux), both Skylake, for the AVX-512 analysis.
stars_or_usage: 545 stars; ipnsort and driftsort are the implementations used by the Rust standard library (per the writeups)
tradeoffs: Generic comparison sorts with panic-safety and Ord-safety care; ipnsort uses branchless instruction-level parallelism and only SSE2, no explicit SIMD; driftsort needs auxiliary memory. For large random primitive inputs the author concedes vqsort (clang) and x86-simd-sort are faster.
caveats: Written by the ipnsort author (bias disclosed in the writeups). The headline comparison with libstdc++, libc++ and MSVC std::sort is shown only in images (assets/stable-hot-u64-10k.png, unstable-hot-u64-10k.png), so the text carries no ratio for it; the quoted ~15x to ~20x figures are against x86-simd-sort on patterns where that library scales badly (random_p5) or cannot exploit sortedness, and the same writeup shows x86-simd-sort faster than ipnsort on random and saw-like input on Linux. Toolchains are from 2023. Sorting is only loosely a numerics-and-arrays task; the orchestrator may re-file it.
found_via: GitHub: sweep of github.com/topics/sorting-algorithms?l=rust, then Voultapher/sort-research-rs README and writeups (sort_safety, intel_avx512, ipnsort_introduction)
why_faster: Per the ipnsort writeup: sorting-network small-sort that avoids branch misprediction, branchless cyclic Lomuto partition (~1.2x overall on u64 on Zen 3), i-cache-aware inlining of only the small-input insertion sort, and pdqsort-style pattern detection that sorts ascending input in O(N).

name: Gaius.jl (Julia multi-threaded divide-and-conquer BLAS-like matmul)
baseline: OpenBLAS gemm (C and assembly) with 6 threads (BLAS.set_num_threads(6)); for integer matrices Julia's generic matmul, since OpenBLAS has no integer matmul
workload: Square matrix multiplication for Float64, Float32 and Complex{Float64} (struct-of-arrays) across a range of sizes, shown as log-log plots.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Gaius outperforms OpenBLAS over a large range of matrix sizes, but does begin to appreciably fall behind around 800 x 800 matrices for Float64 and 650 x 650 matrices for Float32'; Complex{Float64} 'competeing relatively evenly against OpenBLAS'. No numeric ratio is printed; results are plot images.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.4.0-rc2.0 (LLVM 8.0.1, znver1), JULIA_NUM_THREADS=6; OpenBLAS version not stated; built on LoopVectorization.jl.
tradeoffs: Matmul only (README: other BLAS routines not implemented); README says it is 'not stable or well tested' and 'not actively maintained' and points to Octavian.jl (already catalogued) and Tullio.jl as successors; Julia-only.
caveats: Plots only (assets/*.png not opened) and the repo has no benchmark script, so tier C; 2020-era Julia release candidate on a Zen+ CPU without AVX-512; the lead over OpenBLAS ends near 800x800 (Float64), so it is a small and medium size win; author-run. Most useful as a study of a simple pure-Julia matmul.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/blas?l=julia and linear-algebra?l=julia topic pages (Gaius.jl listed), then README
why_faster: Divide-and-conquer task parallelism on Julia's depth-first task runtime with LoopVectorization.jl SIMD kernels (README).

name: Fucina (Zig CPU tensor/autograd runtime and LLM inference engine)
baseline: llama.cpp (ggml, C/C++) CPU-only (llama-bench -ngl 0), build 30af6e2; on macOS with its Accelerate BLAS backend active, on x86 with BLAS off, GGML_NATIVE=ON, GGML_LLAMAFILE=ON, GGML_CPU_REPACK=ON, GGML_OPENMP=ON
workload: Paired same-GGUF, same-thread-count CPU runs of LLM prefill (20 prompt lengths) and decode on Qwen3-0.6B (seven quantization formats incl. f16), Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3.5-0.8B, Qwen3-30B-A3B MoE and Gemma-4-26B-A4B, i.e. quantized GEMM and GEMV kernels.
claimed_speedup: docs/BENCHMARK.md, Apple M1 Max, 8 threads: 'of 236 cells - Fucina faster 221, parity 13, llama.cpp faster 2'; dense prefill per-format geomeans 1.18-1.81x (Qwen3-0.6B f16 1.81x, Q8_0 1.27x, Q4_K_M 1.45x; Qwen3-1.7B Q4_K_M 1.18x); Q4_K_M and Q4_K_S decode 1.15x; Qwen3-30B-A3B large prefill 1.44-2.09x. Intel i9-13950HX: dense Qwen3-0.6B quantized formats 'paired-gate median ratios 1.32-1.95 per format', Q4_K decode 1.21-1.25x. Recorded losses: on x86 llama.cpp is ahead on MoE decode (Fucina 0.90-0.95x of llama.cpp) and Q5_K dense decode (0.90x); on M1 Qwen3.5-0.8B Q8_0 pp32 (0.86x) and Qwen3-30B Q6_K decode (0.88x).
compiler_and_flags: zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast with the default native target (no -Dtarget), Zig 0.16; llama.cpp x86 flags as listed in the baseline field; llama.cpp compiler and optimization flags for the M1 build are not stated (described as its production configuration).
hardware: Apple M1 Max (macOS, 8 threads) and Intel i9-13950HX (Raptor Lake 8P+16E, AVX2 + AVX-VNNI, Linux).
tradeoffs: CPU-first and tuned for Apple Silicon NEON and x86 AVX2/AVX-VNNI; the binary must be built on the machine that runs it (or with -Dcpu); Zig pre-1.0; GPU use is an opt-in offload at the op seam; applications live in the library repo for now.
caveats: Author-run on laptops that are thermally and page-cache sensitive (the author adds a prewarmed paired gate); gemma4 and qwen3.5 rows were best-of rather than mean ('favorable to Fucina - flagged'); llama.cpp moves fast so the 2026-07-04 snapshot ages; on M1 the baseline switches to Accelerate/AMX at batch >= 32, which the doc says costs it heavily at pp32-129 (up to 7.2x for f16 pp32) and inflates prefill ratios; several Fucina kernels are direct ports of llama.cpp/ggml code (README acknowledgements), so the algorithms are not independent. An LLM runtime is only loosely a numerics-and-arrays entry; the orchestrator may re-file it.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/simd?l=zig topic page (fucina listed), then README and docs/BENCHMARK.md
why_faster: README: on CPU per-op dispatch is cheap and kernels specialize at compile time instead of fusing at runtime; BENCHMARK.md attributes llama.cpp's mid-batch prefill loss to its switch to the Accelerate/AMX path at batch >= 32.

name: hpla-rs (Rust faer-based CSR SpMV and Lanczos exp(-A)b) against Eigen, PETSc, oneMKL and PSBLAS
baseline: Eigen CSR and CSC sparse matrix-vector product (C++); also PETSc CSR (C), Intel oneMKL inspector-executor CSR and CSC (C) and PSBLAS (C++/Fortran), single core
workload: Single-core y += A*x on 28 SuiteSparse matrices, plus one-pass and two-pass Lanczos evaluation of exp(-A)b on 15 symmetric matrices, Criterion with 50 samples.
claimed_speedup: No speedup is stated in the README; ratios derived from python/data/summary.csv (derived from page data, geomean of per-matrix time ratios): Rust faer/csr SpMV is 1.12x faster than Eigen CSR (faster on 19 of 28 matrices), 1.20x faster than Eigen CSC and 1.02x faster than PSBLAS CSR, but oneMKL CSR is 1.24x faster than faer/csr (faer wins 4 of 28) and PETSc CSR is 1.23x faster (faer wins 5 of 28). One-pass Lanczos: faer_csr 1.04x faster than Eigen CSR (8 of 15) and 1.21x faster than PSBLAS CSR, PETSc 1.19x faster than faer_csr.
compiler_and_flags: Rust nightly-2026-04-14: opt-level=3, lto=fat, codegen-units=1, panic=abort, RUSTFLAGS=-C target-cpu=native; C/C++ wrappers: clang/clang++ from LLVM 22 with -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -flto; PSBLAS Fortran wrappers: gfortran 14.3.0 -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -ffat-lto-objects; OMP_NUM_THREADS=1, taskset -c 0, MKL linked as mkl_sequential (README).
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6418H (Sapphire Rapids), one pinned core, 2 TiB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.4, Linux 6.8.
stars_or_usage: 4 stars; companion repo of an arXiv paper
tradeoffs: Single core only; the Rust CSR SpMV specialization lives in a fork of faer on Codeberg (lukefleed/faer) pinned in Cargo.toml, not in this repo; needs nightly Rust and a Spack environment with MKL, PETSc and PSBLAS.
caveats: The repo has no LICENSE file in its top-level listing, hence usability reference (upstream faer is already catalogued). The paper it accompanies (arXiv 2606.19213) was not opened; ratios here were computed from summary.csv 'Time estimate (ns)' columns by this agent. The outcome is mixed: Rust beats Eigen and PSBLAS on geomean but loses to oneMKL and PETSc on CSR SpMV and to PETSc on Lanczos (PETSc is linked against oneMKL); per-matrix ratios against PETSc range 0.54-1.47. Benchmarks were run by the author on one machine.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/sparse-matrix?l=rust topic page (lukefleed/hpla-rs listed), then README and python/data/summary.csv
why_faster: README says the Rust side uses a CSR SpMV specialization in a faer fork; no mechanism analysis was reachable (paper not opened).

name: JavaScript (browser JIT engines and Node.js) in Fourmilab floating_point_benchmarks: fbench
baseline: C fbench compiled with GCC 3.2.3 -O3 on Linux (relative time 1)
workload: fbench, a trigonometry-heavy optical ray-tracing kernel; run time per iteration relative to the C version on the same machine, iteration counts adjusted to about five minutes, single-threaded.
claimed_speedup: Relative time (C = 1), values listed in the page order of the engines: Mozilla Firefox 55.0.2 0.372 (about 2.7x faster than C, derived from page data), Safari 11.0 (macOS) 0.424 (about 2.4x, derived), Brave 0.18.36 1.334, Google Chrome 61 1.378, Chromium 60 1.386, Node.js v6.11.3 1.495 (the last four slower than C).
compiler_and_flags: C baseline: GCC 3.2.3 -O3, Linux; JavaScript: the engine versions listed in the claim, no flags.
stars_or_usage: 6 stars; fbench has been ported to many languages since 1980
caveats: The C baseline is GCC 3.2.3 (an old compiler) while the engines tested are 2017 releases, and the machine and CPU are not named (the page says each language was compared with C 'on the same machine'), so the 2.4-2.7x lead is not an equal-footing result; the same table has C++ (g++ 5.4.0) at 0.939 and Modula-2 (GNU Modula-2) at 0.941, only about 6% faster than the old C row, and four of six JavaScript engines are slower than C. The page gives no mechanism. License is Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike per the README (version not stated, LICENSE.md not opened), not an OSI software license.

workload: fbench, a trigonometry-heavy optical ray-tracing kernel; run time per iteration relative to the C version on the same machine.

name: FastTanhSinhQuadrature.jl (Julia tanh-sinh quadrature)
baseline: Cubature.jl (wrapper of the C cubature library, h- and p-adaptive) and Cuba.jl (wrapper of the C Cuba library: Vegas, Divonne, Cuhre) for 2D and 3D integrals; QuadGK.jl and FastGaussQuadrature.jl (Julia) for 1D
workload: Adaptive numerical integration at rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-8 of 1D, 2D and 3D test integrands on [-1,1]^d (endpoint singularities, smooth, oscillatory), @belapsed timings with caches prebuilt.
claimed_speedup: README table, ns per call (derived ratios are derived from page data): 2D x^2+y^2: FTS quad 2153 vs Cubature h 5980 (2.8x) and Cubature p 9098 (4.2x), Cuhre 6.858e4; 2D exp(x+y): FTS avx 5720 vs Cubature p 3.861e4 (6.7x) and Cuhre 6.697e4; 3D x^2*y^2*z^2: FTS avx 2.207e4 vs Cubature p 2.441e4 (1.1x). Not a win: 3D exp(x+y+z): FTS quad 1.069e6 and avx 3.401e5 vs Cuhre 1.795e5 and Cubature h 3.17e5.
compiler_and_flags: Julia (JIT, no flags); REPRODUCIBILITY.md names Julia 1.11 and 1.12 for tests and 1.13 for docs and figures with pinned Manifest.toml files; the README benchmark table does not name the Julia version.
stars_or_usage: 16 stars; JOSS paper draft in the repo
tradeoffs: Tanh-sinh double-exponential rules: best for endpoint-dominated integrands on boxes; AVX interface; GPL-3.0 licence; Julia only.
caveats: Baselines are Julia wrappers around C libraries that call back into Julia integrands, so the comparison mixes algorithm (tanh-sinh versus adaptive cubature and Monte Carlo) with wrapper overhead, and several baseline cells carry '*' (tolerance not met, e.g. Cuba Vegas and Divonne on 2D and 3D, Cubature p on singular cases), which makes their times meaningless for those cases. Author-run on one laptop CPU with samples=3, evals=1; one baseline (Cuhre) is faster on the 3D smooth case. The headline speedup plot (JOSS_paper/benchmark_summary.svg) compares against the fastest accurate method per case, and for 1D that is a Julia package (QuadGK or FastGaussQuadrature), which is not a C baseline.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/simd?l=julia topic page (FastTanhSinhQuadrature.jl listed), then README benchmark table and REPRODUCIBILITY.md
why_faster: Double-exponential (tanh-sinh) node clustering with prebuilt adaptive caches and an AVX interface (README); no mechanism analysis against the C libraries.
